newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish environment group opposes U.S. corn import.
newsitem.headline: Polish environment group opposes U.S. corn import.

text.p: Polish environmentalists, recently stirred by a report alleging inadequate control over genetic engineering in Eastern Europe, are protesting over the arrival of a grain cargo from the U.S.
They say the shipment may contain gene-modified corn.

"The vessel Met Sorento is waiting in the port of Szczecin which has brought 15,000 tonnes of corn from the United States," a spokesman of Poland's Green Federation, Dariusz Szwed, told a news conference on Friday.
Szwed said that as U.S. regulations did not require genetically modified corn to be separated, the cargo might contain such material.
"The Green Federation protests against the spread through the country of this corn, because the effects on those who consume it are unknown," he said.
A duty official at Szczecin port confirmed to Reuters that a vessel called the Met Sorento was due to unload a cargo of maize but further details could not immediately be obtained.

Szwed also criticised a decision by the EU's executive Commission this week to clear genetically modified maize, developed by Swiss firm Ciba-Geigy, to resist the corn borer pest and a powerful weed killer, for sale in Europe.
He said his organisation had recently written to major food manufacturers asking them not to use genetically altered products and had received assurances from one such company.

He echoed concerns among Western environmentalists that genetic alterations could lead to increased resistance of bacteria to antibiotics and could encourage insects to become more resistant to pesticide strains.
He said the federation would demand from Poland's government urgent legislation protecting consumers from genetically altered foodstuffs. @

The international organisation Greenpeace last month issued a report alleging that much of Central and Eastern Europe lacked adequate legal controls on experiments and field trials with genetically engineered organisms.
The report, published by Greenpeace in the Netherlands, focused on Poland and singled out experiments in which carp, containing human genes to make them grow larger, had been kept in ponds.
It suggested such carp might reach the wild, with unpredictable consequences, but scientists involved in such projects denied this was possible, or that there was any risk.

Polish environmentalists say Eastern European countries, still using traditional farm methods, have a unique opportunity to develop exports to the West of organic foods, which could be threatened if genetically altered strains became widespread.
They say cash-starved East European researchers are easily tempted by foreign companies seeking to conduct research which could be hindered by law in their own countries.
